title: Rights Given Up for the Good News
sum: Chapter 9 looks like a detour, but it is the center of Paul's answer about idol meat. He has just said that he would never eat meat again if it made a brother fall (8:13). Now he shows what that looks like in his own life. He is free, an apostle, and he has the same right as Peter and the Lord's brothers to be supported by the churches and to bring a wife along. He has used none of it (9:1-18).

He then explains why. He has made himself everyone's slave in order to win as many as he can (9:19-23): to Jews he lives as a Jew, to those outside the law as one outside the law, to the weak as weak. The chapter ends with two pictures from the games of Corinth, the runner and the boxer, and with a sober fear that he might be disqualified himself (9:24-27). The point for the strong in Corinth is that freedom exists to be given up for others.
readings: Read as an example to copy

Most commentators hold that Paul offers himself as the model for the strong (11:1). He is more free than any of them, and he gives up more. The chapter then belongs to the argument of 8:1-11:1: knowledge says "I may," love says "I will not, for their sake."
Read as a defense of his apostleship

Some Corinthians questioned Paul's standing, perhaps because he refused their money and worked with his hands (9:3, 6, 12). On this reading, 9:1-18 answers critics ("my defense," 9:3), and the point about idol meat is secondary. The two readings are not rivals: the chapter does both.

views.H: Corinth was a city of patrons and clients, where free people would not do manual labor if they could help it. Paul worked in a shop and refused gifts from the rich (9:6, 12), which could look like a refusal of friendship (Marshall). The soldier, vineyard and flock (9:7), the temple and its altar (9:13) and the Isthmian Games (9:24-27) were all familiar sights in a colony that hosted the games.
views.C: Some older scholars (Weiss, Schmithals) thought chapter 9 belonged to a different letter from chapters 8 and 10, since it seems to leave the topic. Most now defend the unity of 8:1-11:1 (Mitchell's rhetorical reading, Fee, Thiselton, Garland). The Byzantine text lacks the clause "though I am not myself under the law" in 9:20 (see the variant), and the order of the questions in 9:1 differs.
views.L: The chapter is built as a speech of defense: questions (9:1-12a), proofs from ordinary life, the law and the temple (9:7-14), a statement of his practice (9:12b-18), and a summary of his method (9:19-23), then an image (9:24-27). The words "win" (kerdaino, five times in 9:19-22), "all" and "right" (exousia) tie it together. Verse 9:22 states the whole in one line: "I might save some."
views.J: Paul argues from Torah (Deuteronomy 25:4), from the temple service (Numbers 18) and from the priests' portions, all Jewish materials, and calls it "the law of Moses." He says he became "like a Jew" to the Jews and "like one under the law" to those under it. Whether he did this as an observant Jew adapting among Gentiles (Rudolph, Nanos) or as a Jew who no longer saw the law as binding (Dunn) is one of the main questions in the study of Paul and Judaism. Jewish scholars such as Fredriksen and Boyarin take part in that debate.
views.T: Chrysostom read the chapter as Paul's training for the strong, a model of giving up rights (Homilies on 1 Corinthians, on chapters 9-10, as reported). Calvin used 9:14 in his commentary to defend the right of ministers to be supported, and that right became part of church order in the Reformed churches. Verse 9:5 has been used on both sides of the debate about clergy marriage (see the card). Verse 9:27 is a key text in the argument about whether a believer can fall away (see the card).

deep.h: Paul and money: why he refused
deep.b:
Paul argues at length for the right of the apostle to be paid, and then says he has not used it. He took money from other churches (Philippians 4:15-16; 2 Corinthians 11:8-9) but not from Corinth. Peter Marshall argued that taking a rich Corinthian's gift would have made him that person's client, and that his refusal was taken as an insult by Corinthian patrons. Another reading is simpler: Paul did not want anyone to say he preached for profit (9:12; 2 Corinthians 2:17). Paul's work also became the model he points to elsewhere (1 Thessalonians 2:9; Acts 20:33-35).

The Christian church later turned the right of 9:14 into the principle that pastors may be paid. Paul's own choice is the example of a free person giving up a right, which is why chapter 9 sits inside the argument of chapters 8 and 10.

deep.h: "All things to all" and Paul's flexibility
deep.b:
Verses 19-23 have been read both as an admired model of missionary flexibility and as a charge of insincerity. Paul says he is free from all and makes himself a slave to all. His examples are cultural (Jews, Gentiles) and moral (the weak). The Plain keeps Paul's own words, "I have become all things to everyone" (tois pasin gegona ta panta), so that the reader can hear the echo of "I do everything" in 9:23 and "in everything" in 10:33. It does not make Paul a chameleon: he changes his practice, not his message or his obedience to God ("I am not outside God's law but under Christ's law").

Augustine and Jerome argued in their letters about whether Paul's behavior here and in Galatians 2 was sincere. Augustine said Paul really did keep Jewish practices as an indifferent custom; Jerome said it was a pretense. The question, on both sides of the modern argument, is what "law" Paul still considers binding.

echoes: Deuteronomy 25:4; Numbers 18:8-32; Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10; 1 Timothy 5:17-18; Acts 18:3; Acts 16:3; Galatians 1:15-16; Galatians 2:11-14; 1 Corinthians 8:13; 1 Corinthians 15:8; Philippians 3:12-14; 2 Timothy 4:7-8

settings.what: Paul's defense of his freedom and the example of giving up his rights
settings.to: The church at Corinth: the strong, who are free to eat idol meat; the weak, whose conscience is troubled; and the critics who questioned Paul's apostleship
settings.when: Within the long answer about idol meat (8:1-11:1), written from Ephesus about AD 53-55
settings.why: To show the strong what freedom looks like when it is used for others. Paul has every right to eat and drink at the churches' expense, to bring a wife and to stop working, and he gives up all of it so that nothing hinders the good news. The same logic is meant to move them to give up their right to eat meat in front of weaker believers. Knowing this changes how 8:13 and 10:23-33 read: Paul asks nothing of them that he is not already doing.
settings.readers: Gentile and Jewish believers in a patronage culture who prized status, knowledge and freedom, and who did not expect a leader to be a worker and a slave
views: Paul gives himself as the model for the strong (11:1).
Paul answers those who judged him by his refusal of pay (9:3).

settings.to: The Corinthian church, in particular those proud of their knowledge and spiritual standing
settings.when: Immediately after describing his own practice, and before the wilderness warning of chapter 10
settings.why: To warn that being in the race does not mean winning it. The Corinthians knew the Isthmian Games and the training they demanded; Paul uses them to say that discipline matters and that he himself could fail. This prepares the example of Israel in chapter 10: a whole people started and many fell.
settings.readers: Greeks who watched or took part in the games held near their city

traditions.q: Paul claims the right to take a wife along like the other apostles (9:5). May ministers marry?
views: Priests of the Latin Church are normally chosen from men who live as celibates for the sake of the kingdom (Catechism 1579). This is a church rule, not a doctrine, and Eastern Catholic churches ordain married men. Permanent deacons may be married.

Married men may be ordained deacons and priests, but a man may not marry after ordination, and bishops are chosen from the unmarried, usually monks. The Council in Trullo (AD 691) set this order for the East.

Priests may marry. The Augsburg Confession (art. 23) argues from Scripture and the early church that the forced celibacy of the clergy was a late rule that led to scandal, and the Lutheran churches ordain married men.
Article 32 says that bishops, priests and deacons are not commanded by God's law to vow single life or to refrain from marriage, and it is lawful for them to marry.

traditions.q: Paul fears being "disqualified" himself (9:27). Can a true believer fall away?
views: Perseverance to the end is a gift no one can merit, and no one should be sure of it apart from a special revelation. Trent cites the warning of 1 Corinthians 10:12 for the one who thinks he stands. A believer can lose grace by mortal sin and be restored by repentance (Catechism 162, 2016).
Salvation is a lifelong struggle in which a person cooperates with God's grace. A believer can fall by sin and return by repentance. Paul's athlete is an image for the ascetic struggle.

A believer can fall from faith, and the Augsburg Confession (art. 12) condemns those who deny that the justified can lose the Holy Spirit. But the elect are kept by God's promise in the Word, and Lutherans warn against both false security and despair (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 11).

True believers "can neither totally nor finally fall away" because God keeps them (Westminster Confession 17.1). Warnings such as 9:27 are among the means God uses to keep them. The disqualification Paul fears is read as the loss of reward or ministry, or as the fate of one who only seemed a believer.
Wesley held that a believer can fall from grace through unbelief and sin and be lost, and that warnings such as 9:27 and 10:12 are real. He also held that God offers restoration to any who return.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, art. 5) says that all true believers endure to the end and will never fall away from the state of grace, though they may fall into sin and be disciplined. Baptist teachers commonly add that those who finally fall away were never truly believers (compare 1 John 2:19); that is a common Baptist teaching, not wording of the confession, and no theologian is cited here. Some Baptists, especially General Baptists, teach that a believer can lose salvation.

title: Lessons from the Wilderness and the Two Tables
sum: Paul now gives a warning from Israel's own history. Every member of the generation that left Egypt was under the cloud, passed through the sea, was baptized into Moses, ate the same spiritual food and drank from the same spiritual rock, which was the Christ (10:1-4). Yet most of them died in the wilderness, because they craved evil, worshiped idols, committed sexual sin, tested the Christ and grumbled (10:5-10). The point is aimed at Corinthians who think their baptism and their Supper make them safe (10:12).

Then he comes back to idol meat. Flee idol worship (10:14). The cup and the bread are a sharing in Christ's blood and body, and the one loaf makes the many one body (10:16-17). Pagan sacrifices go to demons, and a believer cannot sit at the table of the Lord and the table of demons (10:20-21). But meat sold in the market, or served in a home, may be eaten without asking (10:25-27), unless someone makes it an issue of religion (10:28-29). Everything is to be done for the glory of God (10:31).
readings: Read as a warning to the strong

Paul takes away the Corinthians' false confidence. The strong think knowledge (8:1-2) and the sacraments make them safe. Israel had the same signs and fell. The chapter then gives one limit on freedom: no sharing in the worship of idols.
Read as a solution to the idol-meat problem

Chapter 10 puts together a rule that handles three cases: banquets in temples (forbidden, 10:14-22), meat from the market (permitted, 10:25-26) and meals in a private home (permitted unless made an issue, 10:27-30). Some scholars take chapter 10 as Paul's final answer to the Corinthians and chapter 8 as a first, partial one.

views.H: The Corinthian temples had dining rooms that hosted birthdays, weddings and club dinners, and the meat market (makellon) sold meat from the sacrifices. For a Christian with friends, clients or an employer, refusing was a social cost. Christian tradesmen in a city built on honor and connections faced real pressure (Cheung, Gooch, Murphy-O'Connor).
views.C: The relation of chapters 8 and 10 is debated. Johannes Weiss and others thought the two chapters came from different letters, with 8:1-13 and 10:1-22 being incompatible on idol meat; most now defend the unity of the passage (8:1-11:1) as one argument (Mitchell, Fee, Thiselton, Hays). Textual points: 10:9 (Christ, Lord or God), 10:20 ("the Gentiles"), 10:23 and 10:28 (see the variants).
views.L: The structure runs: warning from Israel (10:1-13), command (10:14), proof from the Supper (10:16-17) and from Israel's altars (10:18), the demons (10:19-21), the jealousy of the Lord (10:22), then practical rules (10:23-11:1). The repeated "all" in 10:1-4 (five times) and "not" in 10:5-10 are marked, and the five failures follow the story from Exodus 32 to Numbers 25.
views.J: The wilderness story belongs to Israel, and Paul says "our fathers," drawing his Gentile readers into it. Jewish writers of his day also told of the rock or well that followed Israel (Tosefta Sukkah 3:11; Biblical Antiquities 11:15, as reported), and Philo read the rock as God's wisdom (Allegorical Interpretation 2.86). Paul's "our fathers" and his rule about Israel's altars (10:18) are not a break with Israel; they use Israel's own history as a guide for Gentiles. The Jewish rule on food and idols (Mishnah Avodah Zarah) is stricter than Paul's, and the Jewish believers among the Corinthians may have felt this.
views.T: The fathers took the cloud, the sea, the manna and the water as signs of baptism and the Lord's Supper (Tertullian, On Baptism 9; Augustine and others). Chrysostom (Homilies on 1 Corinthians, on chapter 10, as reported) stressed that these gifts did not save those who wasted them. The Reformation churches used 10:1-12 in different ways: Catholics and Lutherans on the power of the sacraments, Calvin on warning and perseverance, Zwingli and the Baptists on the Supper as a sign. 10:16-17 is a central text for the doctrine of the Supper. The cards below give each church's reading.

deep.h: Five failures, five Old Testament stories
deep.b:
Paul's list can be matched with the books of Moses. Craving (10:6) recalls Numbers 11:4, 34, the graves of craving. Idolatry (10:7) is Exodus 32:6, the feast at the golden calf. Sexual immorality (10:8) is Numbers 25, where Israel joined Moabite women in the worship of Baal of Peor and a plague killed thousands. Testing the Christ (10:9) is the snakes of Numbers 21:5-6. Grumbling (10:10) is the plague after Korah's revolt (Numbers 16:41-49) or the earlier complaints.

The first, third and fourth each ended in a mass death. Paul does not say the Corinthians had done all these things. He chooses the ones that fit the temple banquet: eating and drinking, then play (10:7), then sex (10:8), then daring God to act (10:9). A temple dinner in Corinth could contain all of them.

On the face of it, Paul seems to allow eating in an idol's temple in 8:10 (as something a "weak" person might be wrongly encouraged to do), forbid it in 10:14-22, and allow market meat in 10:25. Scholars have proposed several ways to read it. (1) Chapter 8 is about meals in the temple precinct and chapter 10 repeats the ban from another side (Fee, Garland). (2) The ban in 10:14-22 is stronger because Paul has now explained that the idol feast is a shared table with demons, not just a social event (Gooch, Cheung). (3) Chapters 8 and 10 come from different moments (partition theories; a minority view). The Apostolic Decree (Acts 15:20, 29) bans "things sacrificed to idols," and there is a long debate about whether Paul knew it or held a looser view (see the card).

deep.title: Spec: the repeated "all" as an answer to Corinthian slogans
deep.b: The word "all" or "every" comes five times in 10:1-4 ("all under the cloud... all through the sea... all baptized... all ate... all drank"). In chapters 6 and 8-10 the Corinthians say "all things are lawful" and "all of us have knowledge" (8:1). My suggestion is that the repetition is deliberate: Paul turns the favorite word of the strong against them. All of Israel had the gifts, and all were in the same place, and yet most were struck down. If the slogans were a claim to safety because everyone is included, Paul's "all" shows that being included is not the same as being safe. Fee, Hays and Garland are reported to read the repeated "all" in the same direction, as aimed at the confidence of the strong (not rechecked page by page), so this is less new than a theory; what is mine is only the link to the slogans of 6:12 and 8:1.

echoes: Exodus 13:21; Exodus 14:22; Exodus 16:15; Exodus 17:6; Exodus 32:6; Numbers 11:4; Numbers 16:41-49; Numbers 20:11; Numbers 21:6; Numbers 25:1-9; Deuteronomy 32:17; Deuteronomy 32:21; Psalm 24:1; Acts 15:29; Romans 14:14; Romans 14:20-21; Revelation 2:14; Revelation 2:20

settings.to: The Corinthian church, in particular the strong who were confident of their knowledge and their place in the church
settings.when: After the example of his own self-discipline (9:24-27), within the discussion of idol meat
settings.why: To break the idea that having the sacraments or knowing the truth makes a person safe. Israel received all the gifts and still failed, so the church must not presume. The same chapter makes the wilderness story the church's own story, and ends with a promise that God will not let any test be too much (10:13).
settings.readers: Mostly Gentile believers who were told that the exodus was their story as well

settings.what: Flee idol worship: the two tables
settings.to: The church at Corinth, especially those who attended meals in pagan temples
settings.when: After the warning from Israel, as the center of the answer on idol meat
settings.why: To draw the line that the argument of chapter 8 had left open: a believer may not take part in a meal at an idol's altar, because eating at a table makes one a partner of the one who hosts it. Paul asks them to judge for themselves what the Lord's Supper means (10:15, 16-17), so that they will see what an idol banquet means.
settings.readers: Believers invited to club dinners, guild feasts and family occasions in temple dining rooms

settings.what: Rules for meat from the market and from a home
settings.to: The church at Corinth, the strong and the weak together
settings.when: After the ban on temple banquets, as the last practical word before the section on worship
settings.why: To give the strong a rule they can use: eat what is sold and what is served, asking no questions; if someone says it was sacrificed, do not eat it, for that person's sake. The goal is not to protect Paul's freedom but the good of the other (10:24, 33). Everything is to be done for the glory of God.
settings.readers: Christians shopping in the Corinthian market and invited to meals by unbelieving friends
views: Paul gives the strong a way to use their freedom without making others fall.
Some scholars see a middle line between the weak and strong, with Paul closer to the strong on market meat and closer to the weak on temple banquets.

traditions.q: Israel had a baptism and a spiritual meal and still fell (10:1-12). Do the sacraments guarantee salvation?
views: The sacraments give grace by the act itself when rightly received (ex opere operato, Council of Trent, session 7, canon 8), but they do not replace faith and a changed life. A baptized person can lose grace by mortal sin, and Paul's example of Israel warns against presumption.

The sacraments (mysteries) are real encounters with God, but salvation is a lifelong communion, and a person can fall away. Israel's failure is a warning to those who receive and do not live by what they receive.

Baptism and the Supper are effective because of God's promise, and they are meant to awaken and strengthen faith (Augsburg Confession, art. 13). Received without faith, they do not help; those who eat the Supper unworthily eat judgment.

The sacraments are signs and seals of the covenant. Their grace is "not conferred by any power in them," but by the Spirit's work in those who receive them by faith (Westminster Confession 27.3). Israel's example shows that outward membership without faith saves no one.

Baptism and the Lord's Supper are ordinances, symbolic acts of obedience that picture what Christ has done (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, art. 7). The wilderness generation shows that outward membership without faith and obedience fails.

traditions.q: Does "a sharing in the body of Christ" (10:16-17) mean Christ is present in the bread, or that believers are united as one body? Who shares in it?
views: Sharing in the Eucharist is real communion with Christ's body, and it makes the Church his Body: the Eucharist "makes the Church" (Catechism 1396). Those not in full communion with the Church do not normally receive.

The Church gathered at the Eucharist is the Body of Christ, and the common cup is the sign of unity. The Orthodox do not share the chalice with those outside their communion, because that would claim a unity that does not yet exist.

Christ's true body and blood are truly present and are distributed to those who eat (Augsburg Confession, art. 10), and those who share are also one in faith. The Formula of Concord (Solid Declaration 7) puts it as the body and blood received "in, with and under" the bread and wine, and holds that even unbelievers receive them, to their judgment.

Believers truly share in Christ's body and blood, spiritually, by the Holy Spirit. Calvin cites 10:17 to show that the Supper binds the church in love (Institutes 4.17.38). The bread is a sign and seal, not a change of substance.

Wesley taught that the Supper is a means of grace in which Christ is present by his Spirit, and that Christians should receive it as often as they can ("The Duty of Constant Communion"). Methodists keep an open table.

The Lord's Supper is an ordinance in which the church remembers Christ's death and shows its unity. The "body" in 10:17 is the congregation. The bread and cup stay bread and cup (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, art. 7; compare Zwingli).

traditions.q: Paul lets believers eat market meat (10:25), but the Jerusalem decree banned food offered to idols (Acts 15:29). What binds Christians today?
views: The decree of Acts 15 was a discipline for its time, to keep Jewish and Gentile believers together, and it no longer binds as a rule of diet. Taking part in idol worship remains forbidden, and the Church teaches that scandal to the weak is to be avoided.

The Didache (6:3) already says to keep away from food offered to idols, and the Orthodox canons keep the Apostolic Decree. In practice, the Orthodox treat the ban on blood and strangled meat as part of church law, while ordinary food is not an issue. Fasting rules are the main Orthodox food discipline.
Rules about foods are not binding on the conscience (Augsburg Confession, art. 26), and Christians are free to eat. Love for the weak limits the use of this freedom.

Christian liberty covers matters Scripture leaves indifferent, and "God alone is Lord of the conscience" (Westminster Confession 20.2). Calvin took Paul's rule to be a lasting pattern of freedom limited by love and by the ban on sharing in idol worship (Institutes 3.19).
Jewish believers remain bound by the Torah's rules on idols and food, and the Jerusalem decree is a minimum for Gentile believers. Paul's permission in 10:25-27 is read as addressed to Gentiles.

title: Heads, Hair and the Lord's Supper
sum: Chapter 11 turns from idol meat to two problems in the church's worship. Paul starts with praise (11:2) and then deals with praying and prophesying with heads covered or uncovered (11:2-16). The argument is hard to follow: it uses the word "head" in more than one sense, the creation story of Genesis, "authority on her head," "because of the angels," nature, and finally "we have no such custom." It is the most disputed passage in the letter after 14:34-35.

Then Paul has no praise at all (11:17). When the church comes together for the Lord's Supper, there are divisions: the rich eat and drink first, and the poor go hungry (11:18-22). Paul reminds them of the tradition he received about the night Jesus was handed over, the earliest written account of the Last Supper (11:23-26), and warns that eating in an unworthy way, without discerning the body, has brought weakness, sickness and death (11:27-32). The answer is simple: wait for one another (11:33).
readings: Read as a rule for all churches

Many churches have taken 11:2-16 as a lasting rule about women's covering and men's order, either in cloth or in the principle of orderly distinction between the sexes. Paul's closing appeal to "the churches of God" (11:16) is used for this.
Read as a response to a local problem

Others hold that the passage is about a Corinthian custom (hair, veils, the way a Roman woman appeared in public), and that Paul's real principle is that worship should not shame anyone or confuse the sexes in a culture where hair and dress carried meanings we no longer share (Winter, Murphy-O'Connor, Fee). The principle lasts; the cloth need not.
Read as the Supper's two faces

The meal of 11:17-34 can be read as a failure of love (the poor shamed) or as a failure of reverence (the body not discerned). Paul has both in view: the one who despises the poor despises the body of Christ.

views.H: In Roman Corinth, hair and head coverings carried social meaning: a married woman's veil showed her respectability, men covered their heads for Roman sacrifices, and cropped or loose hair carried other signals (Oster, Winter, Murphy-O'Connor). House churches met in the homes of the well-off, where the wealthier arrived early and the dining room was small (Murphy-O'Connor, Theissen). Chloe's people and others had reported the divisions (1:11).
views.C: The passage 11:2-16 has long been challenged as non-Pauline: William O. Walker argued that 11:3-16 was inserted later, and Philip Payne makes a similar case for 14:34-35. All manuscripts have it, and most commentators accept it as Paul's. The text of 11:24 and 11:29 is expanded in the Byzantine tradition (see the variants). Paul's tradition in 11:23-25 is the earliest account of the Last Supper.
views.L: The first section is built as a chain of arguments: from headship (11:3), to shame (11:4-6), creation (11:7-9), authority and angels (11:10), mutual dependence (11:11-12), nature (11:13-15) and custom (11:16). The second has a frame: Paul's lack of praise (11:17, 22), the tradition (11:23-26), then a warning (11:27-34). The Greek verbs for "judge," "discern" and "discipline" (krino, diakrino, katakrino) run through 11:27-34.
views.J: The Supper's words recall the Passover meal, with its bread and cup, its command to remember (Exodus 12:14; 13:8) and the covenant of Sinai (Exodus 24:8). Jeremiah's "new covenant" (31:31-34) is named in 11:25. Jewish readers note that praying with the head covered is not clearly attested as a custom of men in Paul's day, and later practice differs by community. On the question of women who pray and prophesy aloud, Jewish and Christian traditions have both argued over the same texts: Miriam and Deborah as prophets, and rabbinic rules for women's roles in worship.
views.T: Tertullian wrote two works on veiling (On the Veiling of Virgins, On the Apparel of Women) and read the angels of 11:10 as the fallen angels of Genesis 6. Chrysostom preached on the passage and, as reported, took care not to read "head" as ranking the Son under the Father. Calvin took the covering as a custom suited to Corinth. On the Supper, the fathers read 11:27-29 as a call to preparation, which led in the Middle Ages to rules of confession before communion (the Fourth Lateran Council, 1215, canon 21, required annual confession and Easter communion), and Luther and Calvin each rewrote the order of preparation. 11:23-26 is the biblical center of the long argument over the real presence, the sacrifice of the Mass and the memorial view (Zwingli). See the cards at Matthew 26:26 and Luke 22:19.

deep.b:
The earliest readers took the passage as a rule about veils. Tertullian (about AD 207) wrote that women, and virgins in particular, should be veiled in church and in public. Chrysostom's homily treats the covering as a sign of the woman's honor and the order of creation. In the Middle Ages the Western church required women to cover their heads in church, a rule written into canon law in 1917 (canon 1262) and dropped in the 1983 Code. The Reformers kept the principle of order but not always the cloth: Calvin held that the covering fit a custom of Corinth, and that churches might have other customs. Conservative Anabaptist groups kept the prayer covering as an ordinance.

In the twentieth century, a new debate came over the Greek word kephale and over the sentence "because of the angels." Egalitarian and complementarian scholars now argue over whether 11:3 sets up a lasting order of authority. The card on 11:3 and the card on the covering give each church's view. What is certain is that Paul expects women to pray and prophesy in the gathering (11:5), and that he gives reasons from creation and from custom.

deep.h: 11:17-34: the earliest account of the Last Supper
deep.b:
Paul's letter (about AD 53-55) was written before any Gospel, and it gives the oldest version of the words of Jesus at the Supper. It is close to Luke (Luke 22:19-20), and Mark and Matthew have a slightly different form. Paul says he received it "from the Lord" and handed it on. There are four points to know: (1) the setting is a full meal, with the bread before it and the cup after (11:25); (2) "for you" and "new covenant" tie the meal to Jesus' death; (3) "until he comes" ties it to the future (11:26); (4) the abuse in Corinth was social: the rich eating separately from the poor.

Paul's remedy is plain: examine yourself, wait for one another, and eat at home if you are just hungry (11:28, 33-34). The sentence "if he does not discern the body" is the center of the debate: it can mean the bread, the church, or both.

echoes: Genesis 1:26-27; Genesis 2:18-23; Genesis 6:1-4; Numbers 6:5; Exodus 12:14; Exodus 24:8; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Isaiah 53:12; Matthew 26:26-29; Mark 14:22-25; Luke 22:19-20; Acts 18:7-8; 1 Corinthians 10:16-17; 1 Corinthians 12:12-27; 1 Corinthians 14:34-35; Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 5:23; Jude 12

settings.what: Instruction on heads and hair when praying and prophesying
settings.to: The church at Corinth: women and men who pray and prophesy aloud when the church gathers
settings.when: After the long answer on idol meat; the first of two problems in the church's gatherings
settings.why: To keep the church's worship from shaming anyone in a culture where hair and head coverings carried meaning. Readers differ on what Paul was protecting: the difference between the sexes, the honor of husbands, or the church's reputation among outsiders. Paul praises their faithfulness (11:2), then gives a chain of reasons for a custom the Corinthians were breaking. Knowing that women were praying and prophesying aloud in the assembly changes how this passage is read: Paul does not say they should stop, but that they must do it in an accepted way.
settings.readers: Members of house churches in a Roman colony, where a woman's dress and a man's hair signaled status, marriage and morals
views: A veil or covering for women
The covering is a cloth veil, and Paul requires it (traditional reading).
The issue is long or loose hair and men's hair, with the "covering" being the hair itself (Murphy-O'Connor).
Paul adapts to the dress of respectable Roman women and men at prayer (Oster, Winter).

settings.what: Rebuke and instruction about the Lord's Supper
settings.to: The church at Corinth, in particular the wealthier members who ate before the poor and the church as a whole
settings.when: After a report of divisions in the assembly (11:18), when the church meets for a shared meal
settings.why: To stop a meal meant to proclaim the Lord's death from becoming a place where the rich shame the poor. Paul calls them back to the tradition he gave and to self-examination, so that the meal says what it was meant to say: one body, one table. The setting changes the meaning of "unworthy": it describes how they eat, not who they are.
settings.readers: House-church members of very different wealth: patrons with large dining rooms, and slaves and day laborers who came late
views: The sin was greed and division, the rich shaming the poor (Theissen, Fee).
The sin included not recognizing the bread as the Lord's body (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran readings).

settings.what: The tradition of the Lord's Supper
settings.by: Paul, reporting the words of Jesus on the night he was handed over
settings.to: The Corinthian church; first spoken by Jesus to the Twelve at the meal
settings.when: The night before Jesus' death, passed on to Corinth when Paul founded the church (about AD 50-51) and repeated in this letter (about AD 53-55)
settings.why: To bring the Corinthians back to what the meal was for. By recalling the words and the command to remember, Paul shows that the meal proclaims the Lord's death until he comes, and cannot be a private dinner.
settings.readers: Gentile believers who had no memory of Passover and needed to be told what the bread and cup meant

traditions.q: Must women cover their heads in worship (11:5-6, 10)?
views: The 1917 Code of Canon Law (canon 1262) required women to cover their heads in church. The 1983 Code dropped the rule, and the Catechism does not mention it. Many Catholic women, especially in communities that celebrate the traditional Latin Mass, still wear a veil.

Women customarily cover their heads in church in many Orthodox countries and parishes. This is an inherited custom and a sign of reverence rather than a rule of doctrine. Practice varies, and in many North American parishes it is optional.
Lutheran churches generally do not require a covering and treat the passage as a custom of its time. No confession is cited here.

Calvin held that Paul was settling a custom of Corinth, and that the covering was a sign of order suited to that place; churches elsewhere may have other customs (11:16). Most Reformed churches today do not require it.
Anglican churches generally do not require a covering and treat the passage as a custom of its time. No formulary is cited here.

Old Order Amish, Old Order and conservative Mennonites, and groups descended from the Schwarzenau Brethren (such as the Old German Baptist Brethren) teach that 11:2-16 commands a prayer covering for women and wear it in daily life; other Mennonite groups do not. These are not the Plymouth Brethren. No confession is cited here.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) says nothing about head coverings. Most Baptist churches read the passage as a custom of its time and keep the principle of orderly worship without a cloth; a few teach that a covering is still required.
Most evangelical churches do not require a covering. Plymouth Brethren assemblies, within the wider evangelical world, commonly have women cover their heads at worship and men uncover theirs.
Most Pentecostal churches, such as the Assemblies of God, do not require a covering.

Churches such as the United Pentecostal Church International teach in their holiness standards that women should not cut their hair, taking the long hair of 11:15 as the covering that God gave. The Articles of Faith cited elsewhere do not themselves state this, so no source is given here.

traditions.q: Does "the head of a woman is the man" (11:3) set a lasting order of authority between men and women?
views: Men and women have equal dignity as God's image (Catechism 369-372). The Church reserves ordination to men (Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, 1994), and does not base this only on 11:3; it holds that Christ chose men as apostles.
Men and women are equal in dignity with different roles. Only men are ordained priests and bishops, and headship in marriage is read as sacrificial love (Ephesians 5), not as ranking.

Divided. The Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod teaches that Scripture reserves the pastoral office to men (A Brief Statement, 1932, as reported). The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, and the church bodies that formed it, have ordained women since 1970.

Divided. The Church of England has ordained women priests since 1994 and women bishops since 2015, and some Anglicans who do ordain women read 11:3 with 11:11-12 and Galatians 3:28. Some other Anglican provinces do not ordain women, and the Communion has no single rule.

Divided. The Southern Baptist Convention's Baptist Faith and Message (2000, arts. 6 and 18) teaches that the husband is head of his family and that the office of pastor is limited to men, and that the wife is to submit graciously to his servant leadership. Other Baptist bodies, including American Baptist Churches USA and the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship, ordain women.

Divided. The Presbyterian Church in America holds a complementarian view, with ordained office reserved to men (its Book of Church Order); other Reformed churches, such as the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.), ordain women and read "head" differently.
The United Methodist Church has ordained women since 1956 and reads 11:3 in the light of 11:11-12 and Galatians 3:28.
The Assemblies of God ordains women, citing the Spirit's gifts for sons and daughters alike, and reads 11:5 as showing that women pray and prophesy in the assembly.

Evangelicals are divided between complementarian readings (Piper and Grudem; the Danvers Statement, 1987) and egalitarian readings (Christians for Biblical Equality, 1989), which take 11:11-12 and Galatians 3:28 as the key.

traditions.q: What is eating "in an unworthy way" and "not discerning the body" (11:27-29), and who may come to the Table?
views: Anyone conscious of grave sin must go to confession before receiving communion (Catechism 1385; Council of Trent, session 13, citing 1 Corinthians 11:28). "Discerning the body" is recognizing Christ's real presence in the Eucharist.
Communion is for baptized Orthodox Christians who have prepared with prayer, fasting and confession. To discern the body is to recognize the Eucharist as Christ's body and the Church as his body.

The worthy guest is the one who believes the words "given and shed for you for the forgiveness of sins" (Small Catechism). Many Lutheran churches practice close communion, limited to those who share the Lutheran confession of the real presence.

The table is "fenced": the ignorant and openly ungodly may not come (Westminster Confession 29.8), and everyone should examine themselves. Calvin reads "discerning the body" as honoring the Supper's gift and the unity of the church.

The table is open to all who love Christ, repent and seek to live in peace with each other. Wesley called the Supper a "converting ordinance" and taught that self-examination is for those who come with a seeking heart.
Schleitheim (1527, art. 3) limits the breaking of bread to those baptized as believers and joined in one body. Self-examination and church discipline guard the table.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, art. 7) calls the Lord's Supper a symbolic act of obedience in which members memorialize Christ's death and look for his return. It does not address open or close communion. Baptist churches differ in practice: many welcome all believers, and some limit the table to baptized members of the congregation or of Baptist churches.
